[derived nouns:] A morphophonemic rule then applies to give the new noun the appropriate vowel harmony and tonal patterns: the Noun Class prefix (but not the suffix) harmonizes with the Verb Stem. The prefix is on a Low tone. If the Verb Stem is monosyllabic, then it is ona Mid tone; if it is polysyllabic, then the first syllable is ona Low tone, and subsequent syllables are on Mid tones. The suffix has a Mid or Low tone opposite to the in- herent tone of the final syllable of the Verb Sten.

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: all quoted fragments are verbatim in the held scanned file at the stated line ranges. (2) The deciding source is the 1973 SOAS reference grammar, the fullest description of the language; no later phonology/prosody study of Lelemi exists in Glottolog's list or in any open bibliographic source I could reach, and the one modern paper fetched sources (Fiedler & Schwarz 2009, JWAL, p. 59) restates the three-tone analysis after Hoeftmann 1971 and Allan 1973. (3) The weakness of the record was that its tone-section quote came from badly degraded microfilm scanned with no page numbers. sources.citation: Fiedler, Ines & Anne Schwarz. 2009. Focal aspects in the Lelemi verb system. Journal of West African Languages 36(1-2): 57-73.
sources.quote: 'Lelemi is a tone language with tones having lexical and grammatical function. Höftmann (1971) as well as Allan (1973) propose a three-tone system with a contrast between High, Mid, and Low tone. Contour tones LH and HL by tone combinations are common.' No stress/accent statement (the only 'stressed' in the paper is the verb 'is stressed' = emphasised, p. 60).
